t: for which one is liable to karet. For its punishment is karet when one transgresses it deliberately, without witnesses and without warning (and if one transgressed it with witnesses and warning, some are punished by strangulation, some by stoning, and some by lashes).
except for three transgressions. For although their punishment is karet, one is not liable to a sin offering for transgressing them unintentionally.
the blasphemer. One who curses God (for the laws of the blasphemer see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:7-9).
and the Paschal offering. One who did not bring the Paschal offering at its time.

as it is said, "one of all the commandments of the Lord that should not be done". The correct verse may be: "one of the commandments of the Lord that should not be done" (Leviticus 4:27), or perhaps it is a copyist's error (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 1:2 and R. Yosef Kapach's note there).

and it is said of one who acts unintentionally. This verse was said regarding the sin offering of an individual who served idols unintentionally, and the sin of the blasphemer is similar to the sin of idolatry (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:6).

even though he is liable to karet, and if he acted deliberately he is stoned. Idolatry is among the transgressions for which one is liable to karet. And if he accepted it as a god deliberately (with witnesses and warning), he is actually punished and is liable to stoning, even if he performed no act (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:4). But if he did so unintentionally he is not liable to a sin offering, since he performed no act.

and it is said, "in doing one". In the passage on the sin offering for unintentional sin it says: "And if one person sins unintentionally from among the people of the land, in doing one of the commandments of the Lord that should not be done" (from this, one who sinned without performing an act, such as idolatry, is exempt from a sin offering - Rivash/Rik"v).
for both of them do not bring a fixed sin offering but a variable burnt offering, as will be explained. Below 10:4-5.
as will be explained. Below 10:4.
8) his wife's daughter. From another husband.
11) his sister. And he is liable to karet because of "the nakedness of your sister" (Leviticus 18:9).

12) his sister who is the daughter of his father's wife. His sister born to his father from another mother, and he is liable to karet because of "the nakedness of your father's wife's daughter" (Leviticus 18:11; see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 2:3-4).
16) his father's wife. His stepmother.
22) a male. A man.
26) a woman who brings an animal. She brings the animal upon her to lie with it.
thus all the karet-punishable forbidden relations are twenty-six. For the details of the forbidden relations and their laws see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah chapters 1-4.
1) one who serves idols by an act. See above 5:2.
2) one who gives of his seed to Molech. He hands over his son to the priests who worship fire and then passes him through the flame from side to side (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 6:3).
3) a ba'al ov (necromancer). He appears as if a dead person is speaking, by means of various rituals and incantations (ibid. 5:1).

4) a yid'oni by an act. He speaks, by means of various rituals and incantations, of things that will happen in the future (ibid. 5:2). If he spoke of future events without performing an act, although deliberately he is liable to karet, he is not liable to a fixed sin offering for unintentional sin (see Lechem Mishneh).
9) one who eats forbidden fat. The fat of a pure animal (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:1).
10) one who eats blood. The blood of an animal, beast or bird, whether pure or impure (ibid. 6:1).
11) one who eats notar. The meat remaining from an offering after the time for eating it has ended (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:10).
12) one who eats piggul. From an offering that was disqualified by the intention to eat it at the wrong time (ibid. 13:6).
14) one who offers a sacrifice outside the Temple court. He offers it on an altar outside the court.

15) one who compounds the anointing oil. One who prepares oil like the anointing oil, with the exact quantities of spices that Moses prepared in the wilderness, in order to anoint himself with it (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:4).
16) one who compounds the incense. One who prepares incense according to the weight proportions of the incense that was in the Temple, in order to smell it (ibid. 2:9).
17) one who anoints with the anointing oil. If he anointed himself or others with the anointing oil that Moses made (ibid. 1:5-6).
and what is the offering. What type of animal he brings for his sin offering.

in the portion Shelach Lekha. Numbers 15:27: "And if one person sins unintentionally, he shall bring a she-goat in its first year as a sin offering." The Sages learned that the passage speaks of one who sins unintentionally in idolatry (see Talmud Horayot 8a).
an ordinary person. A simple person.
an anointed priest. A high priest who was anointed with the anointing oil (as below 15:6).

and this is the sin offering of one of the people of the land mentioned in the portion Vayikra. Leviticus 4:27-28: "And if one person from the people of the land sins... in doing one of the commandments of the Lord that should not be done... then he shall bring as his offering a female goat without blemish."

and it is burned. After the slaughter, the sprinkling of the blood and the offering of the sacrificial parts, the remainder is taken out to be burned at the Beit HaDeshen (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:2).

as was explained there. Regarding a king it says: "When a prince sins... then he shall bring as his offering a male goat without blemish" (Leviticus 4:22-23), and the prince is the king (Mishnah Horayot 3:3; see also below 15:6). Regarding an anointed priest it says: "If the anointed priest sins... then he shall offer for his sin which he has sinned a young bull without blemish to the Lord as a sin offering" (ibid. 4:3).

an individual who erred in one of these, or a multitude, etc.. Specifically when no mistaken ruling of a court preceded their acts. But when a mistaken ruling of the court preceded the acts of most of Israel and they acted according to it, each individual among the multitude is not obligated in an offering; rather, one bull is brought from each tribe (as detailed below 12:1).
is exempt from a sin offering. And is also exempt from karet, since he did not act deliberately from beginning to end (Hilchot Shabbat 1:19).

for example, one who carried an object from one domain to another on Shabbat. And he is not liable for the labor of carrying out until he lifts the object from one domain and places it in the other (ibid. 13:1).
committed a transgression. Deliberately.
this is deliberate. And he is exempt from the offering.

for unintentional sin regarding an offering is not unintentional sin regarding these transgressions that carry karet. In contrast to unintentional sin regarding an offering in the case of an oath of utterance, an oath of testimony and an oath of deposit, where an unintentional sin regarding an offering counts as unintentional (Hilchot Shevuot 1:11, 1:13).
he is exempt from a sin offering. And in these cases he is exempt even from a provisional guilt offering, since there is no doubt here whether he sinned or not (as below 8:5).
forbidden fat and notar before him. Both are prohibitions that carry karet (as do his wife who is a niddah and his sister, and Shabbat and Yom Kippur).
Shabbat and Yom Kippur before him, etc.. For example, where Yom Kippur fell adjacent to Shabbat and he did work on one of them and does not know when (see also below 8:5).

he brings a sin offering for whatever it was. Since at some point he himself knew of the sin, even though he has now forgotten it, he became obligated in a sin offering. When bringing the offering he says that the sin offering is for the sin he is liable for, even though he does not remember what it is (Kesef Mishneh).

and it is eaten like other sin offerings that are eaten. Although a sin offering slaughtered for a different sin is disqualified and not eaten (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:6), in this case it is valid and eaten.
in the name of one of them. One of the types of karet prohibitions.
to two burning lamps, one of which he extinguished. On Shabbat.
dishes. Bowls.

one who sins unintentionally without intent. Whose purpose and intent was not to do that particular act, but rather he intended to fiddle and play, and it makes no difference to him whether it is that very thing he is fiddling with or something else (Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 4:3).
in forbidden relations or foods he is liable to a sin offering. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:12, Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 14:12.
he intended to lift the detached item and cut the attached one. And one who detaches transgresses the labor of reaping.

the Torah prohibited only a labor of intention, as we explained in its place. For in the labors of Shabbat, whenever what he planned in his mind was not carried out, he is exempt (Hilchot Shabbat 1:8-11; see also below 7:11).
one who has relations with his yevamah. When a man dies without children, his brother is commanded by the Torah to perform levirate marriage with his wife (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:1).

even though they are two bodies, since his time is pressing he does not scrutinize. Although Shabbat is overridden only for one baby and not for the other, since the mohel is hurried to fulfill the commandment, we do not say that he should have examined and checked which baby is the obligated one.

but if neither of them was fit for circumcision on Shabbat. For example, he circumcised the baby whose time was on Shabbat on Friday, and the next day on Shabbat circumcised the one whose time was Friday (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 19:4), so that on Shabbat there was no commandment to circumcise at all, and he is not considered to have acted with permission.
an expert. A mohel.
toward the end of the day. Close to the end of the day.

and you would be found wounding on Shabbat without fulfilling a commandment. For if he did not complete the circumcision on Shabbat, it turns out that he made a wound in the child without performing a commandment, and one who wounds a person on Shabbat is liable to karet (Hilchot Shabbat 8:7-8).

he is liable to a sin offering, for they warned him. And therefore he is not considered to have acted with permission. But if they did not warn him, he is exempt from a sin offering because he acted with permission.

one who carries out the lulav on the first day of the festival that falls on Shabbat. When the Temple stood, the lulav was taken in the Temple on the first day of Sukkot that fell on Shabbat, and likewise in other places that knew with certainty when Sukkot fell (Hilchot Lulav 7:16).

in order to fulfill his obligation with it. The obligation of the commandment. But if he had already fulfilled his obligation with it earlier, he is liable to a sin offering, since he is not engaged in a commandment and we do not say that he carried it out with permission (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 3:14 and the commentators on Talmud ibid. 41b).
and carried it four cubits in the public domain. For carrying in the public domain is one of the primary labors forbidden on Shabbat and one is liable to karet for it (Hilchot Shabbat 12:8).
one who slaughters the Paschal offering on the fourteenth that falls on Shabbat. For the slaughter of the Paschal offering overrides Shabbat (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:18).
that its owners withdrew their hands. From this offering and were counted for another offering.
or died or became impure before the slaughter. In all these cases it turns out that he slaughtered the Paschal offering on Shabbat not for the sake of a commandment, since it has no owners.
a hidden tereifah. Where the tereifah is only discovered after the slaughter.
because he slaughtered with permission. For at the time of slaughter he had no way of ascertaining these matters, and so there was no duty of inspection upon him, and he acts with permission.
or if it was an evident tereifah. In a visible place, such as one with a perforated skull, severed legs and the like.
slaughtered the Paschal offering on Shabbat not for its own sake, by mistake. For example, he thought it was a peace offering and slaughtered it for the sake of a peace offering.
because the sacrifice is valid. And it counts for him as the Paschal obligation, so there is no transgression here at all, since slaughtering the Paschal offering is permitted on Shabbat.
as we explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 15:1.
by mistake. For example, he slaughtered peace offerings thinking he was slaughtering a Paschal offering, and the law is that they do not count as a Paschal offering.
if they are fit for a Paschal offering. For example, it was a one-year-old lamb designated as a peace offering, which is also fit for a Paschal offering.

he is exempt from a sin offering because he slaughtered with permission. Because they are fit for a Paschal offering and his time is pressing to bring the offering, his mistake is justified; and since these sacrifices are fit for what they are (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:12), he in practice fulfilled a certain commandment and is considered to act with permission (Rivash/Rik"v).

he is liable to a sin offering, for it is not fit for the Paschal commandment. Since it is plain that this kind of animal is not fit for a Paschal offering, he should have known this, and he is not considered to have acted with permission (Rivash/Rik"v).

not for those who will eat it, or not for those counted for it, or for the uncircumcised or the impure. In all these cases the Paschal offering is invalid (Hilchot Korban Pesach 2:5), so that he fulfilled no commandment at all by slaughtering it and is not considered to act with permission.
he is exempt, for the Paschal offering is valid. As explained there, so that he fulfilled a commandment by slaughtering the Paschal offering.
one who slaughters communal offerings on Shabbat not for their own sake. For example, he offered the daily offering or the Shabbat additional offering for the sake of another offering.

he is liable to a sin offering. For it is plain and known that only communal offerings are offered on Shabbat, so he is not considered to have acted with permission (similar to one who slaughters for the Paschal offering sacrifices that are not fit, as above, halakhah 12).
and he shall burn the sacrificial parts in the evening. He shall offer the portions of the offering that go up on the altar after Shabbat ends.
slaughtered more than the day's obligation. Slaughtered more than the number of communal offerings for that day.
he is liable to a sin offering for the excess. Since the number of communal offerings is known, he is not considered to have acted with permission (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 6:5).

slaughtered individual offerings that do not override Shabbat... is liable to a sin offering. Because the slaughter of individual offerings that have no fixed time does not override Shabbat (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:9).

and the meat is permitted for benefit. Although he committed a prohibition by slaughtering on Shabbat, the meat is not thereby forbidden, so that if he went ahead and sprinkled the blood, it will be permitted to eat (Arukh HaShulchan 208:23; see also Me'iri/Marei Kohen).

and one does not sprinkle the blood. There is a shevut prohibition (rabbinic) against sprinkling the blood, and this shevut was not permitted on Shabbat for offerings that may not be offered (Talmud Beitzah 20b).

and he shall burn the sacrificial parts in the evening. If he went ahead and sprinkled the blood on Shabbat, the offering is valid. However, its sacrificial parts may not be burned on Shabbat, and one must wait until after Shabbat and then burn them (for a similar law see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:19).
lean. Thin.
whether a sin offering. For example, the new moon fell on Shabbat and the new moon sin offering goat must be offered.
whether a burnt offering. The daily burnt offering or the burnt offering of the additional offerings.

and not only that, but we tell him: bring the fat one and slaughter it at the outset. Because one should beautify offerings and offer the choicest (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:1). And although by slaughtering the fat one he causes the lean one to go to burning and retroactively makes its slaughter on Shabbat unnecessary, since it is a mitzvah to choose the best, there is no concern about this (see Keren Orah, Menachot 64a).
but if he slaughtered the fat one first and afterwards the lean one, he is liable to a sin offering for the excess. As above, halakhah 13.

since he lifted up a baby, he is exempt from a sin offering. Since he performed a permitted act, even if a forbidden act was also done with it, he is exempt from a sin offering (see also Hilchot Shabbat 2:16).

even though his intention was only to trap, because he acted unintentionally. Only when his intention to trap was unintentional; since in practice he performed a commandment, he is exempt from a sin offering. But if he intended to trap deliberately, even if he lifted up a baby he is liable to karet (Migdal Oz and Tzafnat Pa'neach, Shabbat, ibid.).
for he did not perform a commandment by this eating. So that his eating is not considered to have been done with permission.
and they did not warn him. Before he sinned. But if they warned him before he sinned, he is deliberate and liable to lashes and exempt from the offering.
he is as one who says: I did not eat unintentionally but deliberately, who is exempt from the offering. For we interpret his words in a way that does not deny the witnesses (see below 9:4, 11:8).
he denied. He rejected, denied.

even if one woman said to him, etc.. Although a woman is disqualified from testimony (Hilchot Edut 9:2), here, where he obligates himself by his silence, even through a woman he becomes liable to a sin offering.

one witness said to him: this is forbidden fat, and he was silent, he must bring a sin offering. For his silence constitutes an admission that it was indeed forbidden fat. But if he denied it and claimed that it was not forbidden fat, he is exempt from a sin offering.
and if they warned him. Two witnesses.

he receives lashes for it even though the main testimony is of one witness. For two witnesses are required to obligate lashes only regarding the warning and the testimony to the performance of the act, but for establishing the prohibition one witness is sufficient (Hilchot Sanhedrin 16:6).
in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 15:6.
more than this they said. That even if he set aside a sin offering for that same type of sin, he cannot bring it for a sin he committed at another time.
as was explained there. That a sin offering whose owners died is left to die and the heirs cannot offer it for their own sin (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1).

let him offer whichever he wishes, etc.. Similar to a person who set aside two sin offerings as a safeguard, so that if one is lost he will offer the other, who offers whichever he wishes and the other is left to pasture until blemished and its value is used for a freewill offering (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:5).

brought two sin offerings for two sins, etc.. And he does not know which sin offering he set aside for which sin, for example the animals got mixed up or he forgot which animal he set aside for which sin, and the law is that each offering is slaughtered for the sin for which it was originally consecrated (see Chazon Yechezkel and Chazon David on Tosefta Keritot 2:4). Some explain that this refers to a case where at the time of consecrating the sin offerings he did not specify for which sin each would come, and in this case at the time of offering he may specify which sin offering is for which sin, or he offers each sin offering without specification for whatever it is (see Kiryat Sefer, Rivash/Rik"v, Arukh HaShulchan 209:21-22).
to spite. He transgresses the prohibition out of contempt and rebellion.
as we explained. Ibid.
in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 3:4.
we do not accept from him a sin offering for that sin. But for another sin we do accept from him.
out of appetite. That he transgresses this prohibition because of his desire and not as rebellion.
and regained his sanity. Returned to his right mind.

even though the offering was set aside in the meantime. For during this time the offering was rejected from being offered, since the offering of an apostate is not offered (as above, halakhah 7) nor that of a madman (for a person's sin offering is offered only with his knowledge and will, and a madman has no mind - see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:10).
it has returned and become fit. For now it is fit to be offered.
for living animals are not permanently rejected. Animals that were fit for an offering and were disqualified are not disqualified forever, and if they become fit again they are valid for offering.
as we explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 3:23; see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:4.

and just as if a passing blemish developed in it and healed, it returns to its validity. In contrast to a permanent blemish, which, if it developed in a sacred animal, causes it to be redeemed and become unconsecrated, with a passing blemish one waits until the animal heals and then offers it (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:6-7).
and definite guilt offerings. A guilt offering that comes for a definite sin (see below 9:1).
provisional guilt offerings. A guilt offering that comes for a doubtful sin among those for which one is liable to a fixed sin offering for unintentional transgression (below 8:1).
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.

for any sin that none but the Lord recognizes, is atoned for. This is a sin for which one is liable to a provisional guilt offering, where the owner does not know with certainty whether he sinned, but only the Holy One, blessed be He, knows.

he is exempt from a provisional guilt offering. And if he learned of his sin after Yom Kippur, he is liable to a sin offering, like the law of one who brought a provisional guilt offering and later learned of his sin.
you learn that one does not bring a provisional guilt offering for something unknown on Yom Kippur. Even if he learned of his doubtful sin after Yom Kippur.
as will be explained. In the next halakhah.
one who scorns. One who disrespects offerings and rejects their purpose in his mind or speech.
they hold back the atonement. For the owners' sin is not atoned for until they bring the guilt offering.

except the guilt offering of a nazirite. For a nazirite who became impure must bring on the eighth day of his impurity a sin offering, a burnt offering and a guilt offering, and once he has brought the sin offering he can already begin counting a new term of naziriteship even before bringing the guilt offering (Hilchot Nezirut 6:12).
a doubtful nazirite. Who is uncertain whether he became impure.

and a doubtful person lacking atonement. The four who lack atonement are: the zavah, the woman after childbirth, the zav and the leper, and they may not eat sacred offerings until they bring their offering (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1); and when they are uncertain about their impurity, they must bring a bird sin offering out of doubt (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:6).

and a doubtful sotah. A woman whose husband warned her and she secluded herself, and who claims she is pure, brings a meal offering of jealousy (called a doubtful sotah because there is doubt whether she became defiled or not - Rashi, Keritot 26a).
all of them bring their offerings after Yom Kippur. For their offerings do not come to atone for a sin (Talmud Keritot 26a; see also Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:11).

and he is going out to be put to death by the court. For besides the sin for which he became liable to a sin offering or guilt offering, he committed a transgression punishable by court-imposed death.
if his sacrifice was already slaughtered. The offering was slaughtered before his sentence was finalized.

we delay him until the blood is sprinkled. Because this delay is brief and does not constitute a delay of justice toward the owner of the offering; but if his sentence was finalized before the slaughter, this is a long delay and constitutes a delay of justice, and therefore he is not delayed (Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:5).
in one lapse of awareness. He committed many transgressions without becoming aware between one act and the next that he had done something forbidden, and afterwards he became aware.
these forty-three that we have enumerated. Forty-three transgressions for which one is liable to a sin offering for unintentional sin (above 1:4).
many names. Several types of transgressions.

he is liable for each and every name, etc.. Although generally a prohibition does not take effect on top of another prohibition and a person is not liable for several prohibitions together, in the cases mentioned here a person can become liable for several prohibitions together (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:8).
provided that all the prohibitions come at once. That the prohibitions take effect simultaneously.

or an additional prohibition. Where the later prohibition adds a further stringency to the first prohibition (as below regarding the niddah prohibition for the brother's wife; for further examples see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 14:18-19, Hilchot Terumot 10:25).

or an inclusive prohibition. When the second prohibition includes additional things that had been permitted to the person, this prohibition also takes effect on the thing that was already forbidden for another reason. For example, one who eats the sciatic nerve of an animal that died of itself: initially the animal was permitted to eat and only the nerve was forbidden, and after the whole animal was forbidden as a carcass the nerve was also included in this prohibition, and one who eats it is liable for two (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:6).

like one who says: at the completion of the slaughter he worships it. So that only at the completion of the slaughter does he transgress the prohibition of idolatry, and this prohibition takes effect together with the desecration of Shabbat and the prohibition of slaughtering sacrifices outside.

once he slaughters a little of it for the sake of idolatry it is forbidden. For by performing any act on the animal for the sake of idolatry it becomes forbidden and the one who does so is defined as one who serves idols, and there is no need to cut both organs or the majority of them (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1).
two or the majority of two. Of the signs of slaughter (the windpipe and the gullet), which is the minimum for slaughter of an animal (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9).
for he is not liable for it as one who slaughters outside. So that he is liable to only two sin offerings, for idolatry and for desecrating Shabbat.
as we explained in Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 18:6, that one is liable only for slaughtering outside sacred animals that are fit for the altar.
it was a bird sin offering. And he slaughtered it outside the Temple court.

and half of its windpipe was damaged and he added to it any amount on Shabbat for the sake of idolatry. By this addition he is considered to have slaughtered the bird for the purposes of slaughtering sacrifices outside, since a bird is permitted when the majority of one organ is cut (either windpipe or gullet - Hilchot Shechitah 1:9-11), and at the same time he desecrated Shabbat and transgressed the prohibition of idolatry.

and because of niddah, which is an additional prohibition. For in the prohibition of niddah a stringency is added in one respect, since she is forbidden even to her own husband, and therefore this prohibition is added to the prohibition of a married woman and of a brother's wife.
one who has relations with his father... and likewise one who has relations with his father's brother is liable for two. For these are two prohibitions that come together.
even though they are two bodies. The one who has relations and the one with whom relations are had, and in each case another body performed the act of relations.

the lying one and the one lain with are one name. For these are two sides of the same forbidden act. But if he had relations with Reuven and caused Shimon to have relations with him, he is liable to two sin offerings, for these are two separate acts (as below 5:3).
Laban. The father of Rachel, wife of Jacob.

and Laban has no daughter but Rachel alone. This speaks of a case where Zilpah is not Laban's daughter, and therefore he is permitted to marry her. For had she been his daughter, Tamar, her daughter's daughter, would be forbidden to him (Arukh HaShulchan 212:8, and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 3:5).
and his wife's sister from her father. For Serach and Rachel, wife of Jacob, are sisters from the same father.
and these are two prohibitions that come at once. For both prohibitions took effect at Serach's birth.
to Reuben. Son of Jacob, and she is permitted to him since she is his sister's daughter.
and she became forbidden to the other sons of Jacob. For she is forbidden to them as a brother's wife.

an additional prohibition was added for Jacob, and she is his daughter-in-law. Although a prohibition does not take effect on top of a prohibition, since through this marriage an additional prohibition took effect on Serach with respect to the other sons of Jacob (the prohibition of a brother's wife), and at that moment she also became forbidden to Jacob as his daughter-in-law, the prohibition of a daughter-in-law also takes effect on Jacob by virtue of the additional prohibition, since an additional prohibition takes effect even when it involves two different prohibitions of kinship (but the fact that this woman is forbidden to everyone as a married woman does not cause any of the kinship prohibitions to be added through an additional prohibition, because a married woman is not a kinship prohibition - Shiurei R. Shmuel, Yevamot 32b, and for a similar explanation see Shitah Mekubetzet, Keritot 14b in the omissions).

to Jacob's brother from his mother. Specifically from his mother; for if Jacob's brother from his father Isaac had married her, there would be no possibility of her falling to Isaac for levirate marriage (as mentioned shortly), since she is his daughter-in-law and there is no levirate marriage with her by Torah law (Kesef Mishneh).
since she became forbidden to the other brothers of Jacob. With the prohibition of a brother's wife, this prohibition also takes effect on Jacob (an additional prohibition).
to Ishmael. Brother of Isaac, father of Jacob.

since she became forbidden to the other brothers of Ishmael, an additional prohibition was added for Jacob, the wife of his father's brother. When she married Ishmael she became forbidden to his brothers by the prohibition of a brother's wife, and at that same moment she also became forbidden to Jacob as the wife of his father's brother (an additional prohibition).

and Isaac went and performed levirate marriage with her even though she is a second-degree relative to him. Although Serach, who is his son's daughter's daughter and also his son's daughter-in-law, is not forbidden to him by Torah law, she is among the "secondary" relations, whose prohibitions are rabbinic (see Hilchot Ishut 1:6). And the Sages decreed that secondary relations should not undergo levirate marriage but only chalitzah (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 6:10), and Isaac went ahead and performed levirate marriage with her.
since she became forbidden to his other brothers. Of Isaac, as a brother's wife.
when she is a niddah. And the niddah prohibition, because it applies to her with respect to her husband, is added also for Jacob (as above, halakhah 1).
in the lifetime of Isaac her husband. But after his death he is not liable as for a married woman.
and in the lifetime of Rachel, wife of Jacob. But after her death he is not liable for his wife's sister.
but if they are not present, etc.. For example, if Reuben married Serach and Jacob had no sons except Reuben, the prohibition of a daughter-in-law would not take effect on Jacob.

one who was married to three women, etc.. For example, Leah had two daughters, Dinah and Jochebed, and a son, Asher. And Caleb married three women: Dinah, Miriam daughter of Jochebed daughter of Leah, and Serach daughter of Asher son of Leah (and a man is permitted to marry a woman and her mother's sister, and a woman and her father's sister). And Caleb unintentionally had relations with Leah, who is the mother of Dinah, the grandmother of Miriam, and the father's mother of Serach (Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 3:6).

and there are three names, but it is one prohibition coming at once. For example, he betrothed the three women at once (receiving an agent, or one of them receiving the betrothal for all), so that the three prohibitions took effect on him at once (Har HaMoriah, Arukh LaNer, Keritot 15a).

Scripture made three bodies as one body. Although Scripture specified the three prohibitions, it ended in the singular - "it is lewdness" - for the essence of this prohibition is the union between one mother and her descendants (see Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

he is liable to three sin offerings. Although in the case mentioned in the previous halakhah he is liable to one sin offering for three prohibitions in one body because Scripture made the similar prohibitions between a mother and her descendants as one prohibition, in this case, although these are prohibitions of brotherhood, which are similar prohibitions in one body, Scripture revealed that he is liable to a sin offering for each and every prohibition (Shitah Mekubetzet, Keritot 15a).
and this woman who was had relations with had awareness between each act of relations. She became aware between the acts and then erred again.
he brings one sin offering. For he had no awareness in the interim.
and she brings one for each act of relations. For she had awareness between one act and the next, and the awarenesses divide.

even though all are of one name, since they are separate bodies. Although this is one type of prohibition and one lapse of awareness, since he transgressed the prohibition each time with a different body, he is liable for each time separately.
for what the Sages said: one who has relations with a male and caused a male to have relations with him in one lapse of awareness is liable to one sin offering. See above 4:1.

whether on her own. For example, two witnesses came and testified that her husband died, in which case she does not need the court's permission to remarry (see Mishnah Yevamot 10:1-2 and the commentators there).

by the court. For example, only one witness testified that her husband died and she needs the court's permission to remarry, and even if the court instructed her to remarry, it is considered an error for which a sin offering is owed (as below 14:3).
she is liable to one offering. Because she married one man and this is one type of prohibition in one lapse of awareness, even if her husband had relations with her many times.
or committed fornication with many men. Without marriage, and now it became known that she was a married woman.

for this period of niddah is separate from the second period of niddah, and they are like two niddah women. For when the woman purified herself by immersion and then became impure again, although it was in one lapse of awareness, the days of purity in between make her a separate body.
not at the time of her expected period. Not at the time when she is expected to see menstrual blood.
and she saw blood at the time of relations. So that it turns out he had relations with a niddah, which is a prohibition carrying karet (as above 1:4).
cloth. A cloth with which one wipes the intimate organs after relations.
exempt. For one who is compelled is exempt from a sin offering.
went in to her close to her expected period. For it is forbidden for a man to have relations with his wife during the time when she is expected to see menstrual blood (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:12-13).
and he supposed. Thought.
for this is unintentional error. For he should have checked and been careful to refrain from relations at this time.
if blood was found on his cloth. That he wiped himself after relations and found blood, which proves that this blood came at the time of relations.
both are impure. For one who has relations with a niddah becomes impure as a niddah (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 3:1).
she wiped herself. She cleaned herself by passing a cloth over the place.
and did not wait. She did not delay, for example she had a cloth available and wiped immediately after relations.
both are impure and liable to an offering. For this blood certainly came at the time of relations.
both are impure in doubt. For we are uncertain whether this blood came at the time of relations or afterwards.
and let her wash her face. Let her wash the place of relations, which the Sages call by the euphemism "face" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 2:3).
her husband is pure. For in this case we do not suspect that this blood came at the time of relations, and therefore her husband is pure and they are not liable to an offering.
he must not withdraw while he is erect. He must not remove the organ while it is hard, because he also derives pleasure on withdrawal and is considered to be having relations with the niddah.

as we explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah. 4:11; that he must plant his toenails in the ground and wait without moving until his organ softens, and then withdraw (and this law applies also to one who had relations with his wife not at the time of her expected period, where although he is not liable to a sin offering for entering, since he was compelled, if he withdraws with a live organ he becomes liable to a sin offering for withdrawing).
one for his entry, for he had relations with a niddah. For he had relations close to her expected period and this is defined as unintentional error.
for his withdrawal. The removal of the organ.

for he has two lapses of awareness. One lapse in his entry, for he thought he would manage to have relations before she saw blood, and one in his withdrawal, for he did not know that it is forbidden to withdraw while hard. And he is liable to two sin offerings because there are two different types of unintentional error here, since the error of entry is a practical error about whether he would manage to have relations or not, whereas the error of withdrawal is an error in knowledge of the law (R. Yosef ibn Migash, Shevuot 17b; Rivash/Rik"v).
they are one unintentional error. For both errors are of the same type, an error in knowledge of the law regarding relations with a niddah.
and withdrew while he was still erect immediately. He withdrew immediately while his organ was still hard.
for it is all one unintentional error. An error in knowledge of the law.
like the law of unintentional error in acts of relations. Which was explained above 5:1.
of one name. One type of prohibition.
even though they are in three dishes. In different bowls, even if they were cooked differently (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 3:2).
but if he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat and became aware. He ate unintentionally and afterwards became aware.
and ate again. Unintentionally.
ate half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat. And he is not liable to karet or a sin offering until he eats a full olive-bulk.

provided that he did not pause between them longer than the time of eating three eggs. That from the beginning of the first eating until the end of the second he did not pause for the time of eating three eggs (called "the time it takes to eat a peras"); but if he paused longer than this, he is exempt.
as we explained in Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot. 14:8.
for just as the measure combines for a deliberate transgressor for lashes. For he is liable to lashes if he ate an olive-bulk of the forbidden thing within this time span.
notar. The meat remaining from the offering after the time for eating it has ended, and one who eats it is liable to karet (above 1:4).
from five sacrifices. Five offerings.
and the bodies of the sacrifices do not divide. The fact that these are five different animals does not affect the liability for a sin offering.
for one who eats meat from many sacrifices or from one sacrifice, their law is the same. Their law is equal.
outside. Outside the Temple court.
one who bows to five forms. One who bows to five different idols.

and received it in two cups and drank both in one lapse of awareness brings only one sin offering. For just as the dishes do not divide and the bodies of the sacrifices do not divide, so too the cups do not divide (see Arukh LaNer, Keritot 22a).
if they were gathered through an additional prohibition, or an inclusive prohibition, or a prohibition coming at once. See above 4:1.

therefore an impure person who ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat that was notar on Yom Kippur, etc.. Initially the olive-bulk was forbidden to him as forbidden fat, while the person was permitted to eat the rest of the meat. After the person became impure, eating all the meat became forbidden to him, and the fat was included in this prohibition (an inclusive prohibition), and now eating it carries a prohibition as forbidden fat and as an impure person eating sacred food. And after the fat became notar, a prohibition was added to it, as it is now also forbidden to offer on the altar, and for this reason the prohibition of notar also takes effect on eating the fat (an additional prohibition). And since he ate it on Yom Kippur, on which all eating is forbidden, this fat is included in the prohibition of Yom Kippur (an inclusive prohibition), and he is liable also for eating on Yom Kippur (Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 3:4).
provided that other food is combined with this olive-bulk until it completes a date-sized amount. For this is the measure of forbidden eating on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Shevitat Asor 2:1).

and he brings a definite guilt offering for misappropriation. For before the animal was consecrated the fat was forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit, and when it was consecrated it became forbidden for benefit as well, and since a prohibition of benefit was added to it, a prohibition was added also on eating it (an additional prohibition - Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
eating and drinking are one. See also Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:4.
one who does work on Yom Kippur, etc.. See also above 4:1.
as we explained in Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot. 14:5.

and there is awareness for a half measure. Just as awareness divides between two measures of the same prohibition and obligates two sin offerings, so it divides between two half-measures so that they do not combine to obligate a sin offering.
adjacent to it. For he is not liable until he writes two letters adjacent to each other that can be pronounced together (Hilchot Shabbat 11:11).
is exempt from a sin offering. For the awareness between letter and letter, which is a half-measure, divides.

and likewise two cubits unintentionally, two cubits deliberately and two cubits unintentionally. For he is not liable until he carries four cubits in the public domain, and his awareness in the middle divides and causes there to be no full measure here.

if by throwing he is liable... for it is not in his hand to bring it back, and therefore the awareness in the interim did not help him. Since after the throw began the object is no longer in his hand and the act completes on its own, only his awareness at the time of the throw is considered.
for the awarenesses divide. Even in this case, where there is no awareness between the eatings, since the awarenesses afterwards were separate from each other, he is liable for two.

and so it seems to me that the same law applies to acts of relations. Although relations differ from eating, since in relations it is one body (for example, he had relations with his wife the niddah twice in one lapse of awareness) whereas in eating there are different pieces, nevertheless in acts of relations too, if he became aware separately, he brings two sin offerings (Kesef Mishneh).
even though it is in his lapse of awareness. For they share one lapse of awareness.
for he became aware of part of the first lapse. And therefore the first half olive-bulk is attributed to the first full olive-bulk.

and brought a sin offering for the first, the first and second are atoned for. This speaks of a case where he brought his sin offering before he became aware of the second; but if he became aware of the second before bringing an offering, he is liable to two sin offerings, for awarenesses divide as above 5:9 (Kesef Mishneh, and see below 7:10; and see Arukh HaShulchan 215:11-16, who brought further explanations to distinguish between the halakhot).
but the third is not atoned for. Because the first and third olive-bulks were in separate lapses of awareness, the third is not atoned for by the sin offering of the first.

for awareness of doubt that he had in the interim, although it divides for guilt offerings. For if he became aware between two eatings and is uncertain about both whether he ate forbidden fat or permitted fat, he must bring two provisional guilt offerings (as below 8:7-8).
does not divide for sin offerings. For only definite awareness divides for the purpose of liability to a sin offering, and not awareness of doubt.

one who bows to idolatry, pours a libation, burns incense and sacrifices. One who serves any kind of idol with these four services is liable even if this is not its way of service (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:3).
in one lapse of awareness. He knew it was an idol but forgot that these services are forbidden.
is liable to four sin offerings. For the different services divide for the purpose of liability to a sin offering even though he did them in one lapse of awareness and to one idol.
and likewise if he exposed himself to Peor and threw a stone at Markolis in one lapse of awareness. These services are the special way of serving Peor and Markolis (ibid. 5:2).
is liable to two. Although in both cases he is liable for the prohibition of idolatry in its way of service, he is liable to two because there are different services here (Minchat Chinukh 26:1).
in what case does this apply. That he is liable to a sin offering for each and every service.
when he acted deliberately regarding idolatry. For he knew that it is forbidden to serve idols.
and erred regarding these services. For he did not know that these services are forbidden or did not know that one is liable to karet for them.

he is liable to two... he is liable to only one sin offering. When the error is in the types of forbidden services, he is liable for each and every service, but when the error is in the essential prohibition of idolatry, he is liable to one sin offering.

anyone who forgets the essence of Shabbat and forgets that Israel were commanded about Shabbat. He forgot that there is a prohibition against working on Shabbat, although he knows that this day is Shabbat (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 7:1).
or was taken captive as a minor among the gentiles or converted as a minor while among the gentiles. And has not yet learned about Shabbat and the other commandments.

and likewise all similar to these transgressions. Where there is a single negative commandment and he erred about the essence of the commandment, he is liable to one sin offering even if he did it many times.
is liable to one sin offering for the whole day. For the whole day is defined as one unintentional error.

and likewise a sin offering for each and every Shabbat on which he erred. And it is not enough for him to bring one sin offering for all the Shabbatot, because the weekdays between one Shabbat and the next divide the Shabbatot and make them separate bodies (see below, halakhah 9).
in one lapse of awareness. That he did not become aware between one labor and another that he had done a forbidden labor or that one is liable to karet for this labor.
is liable to only one sin offering. Although he erred about the labors, since he forgot that the day is Shabbat, he is liable to one sin offering for the whole day.

one who does a primary labor and its derivatives in one lapse of awareness. He knew that the day is Shabbat and erred about the primary labor and its derivatives, for example he ground, and also cut vegetables and filed a metal ingot, which are derivatives of the labor of grinding (Hilchot Shabbat 7:7-8).
is liable to only one sin offering. For the derivative is included in the primary labor for the purposes of the sin offering, and he need not bring a separate sin offering for it.
it seems to me that he is liable to two sin offerings. And he is judged as one who did two primary labors in one lapse of awareness, who is liable to two sin offerings.
many labors of the likeness of one labor. Labors of the same nature as a primary labor, which are included in it and are not defined as derivatives (see Hilchot Shabbat 7:2-4).
and layered. He planted in the ground a shoot still attached to a tree in order to grow a new tree from it.
and grafted. He joined a cutting or branch to the stock of an already planted tree. And all these are of the nature of the labor of sowing.
and this has already been explained in Hilchot Shabbat. 7:1-6.
he knew that the day was Shabbat and sowed on it, etc.. This is an example of deliberate Shabbat violation and unintentional error about the labors over many Shabbatot.
even though they are of the likeness of one labor. And had he done all of them on one Shabbat he would be liable to one sin offering.

because the Shabbatot are like separate bodies. And just as one who has relations with many forbidden relations of the same name is liable for each one even though the act of prohibition is the same, because the bodies are separate (for example, he had relations with his five wives while niddah in one lapse of awareness, as above 5:3), so too one who does a labor of the same nature (or even the same labor itself) on separate Shabbatot, each Shabbat is a unit in itself and he is liable to a sin offering for each labor (Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 3:10).
he erred that the day was Shabbat and sowed on it, etc.. This is an example of unintentional error about Shabbat and deliberate performance of labors over many Shabbatot.

for the days between one Shabbat and the next are like awareness to divide. Although he had no awareness between one Shabbat and another, the weekdays between the Shabbatot divide and he is liable to a sin offering for each and every Shabbat (similar to one who had relations with his wife the niddah, and she became pure from her niddah state and he had relations with her a second time after she became a niddah again, where the periods of niddah divide, as above 5:5 - Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 3:10).
one who reaped and ground the size of a dried fig. Which is the smallest measure for which one is liable for these labors (Hilchot Shabbat 8:3, 8:15).
in unintentional error about Shabbat and deliberate performance of labors, he is liable to only one sin offering. When he did them on one Shabbat.

and he became aware of the reaping in the case of unintentional error about Shabbat and deliberate labors. And this awareness obligates one sin offering which also exempts the grinding done with it, since in unintentional error about Shabbat he brings one sin offering for all the labors he did.

reaping draws reaping and grinding draws grinding. The reaping and grinding of unintentional error about Shabbat and deliberate labors draw the reaping and grinding of deliberate Shabbat violation and unintentional error about labors.

and when he becomes aware of them afterwards he need not bring another sin offering. But if he became aware before bringing a sin offering, the awarenesses divide and he is liable to a separate sin offering for unintentional error about Shabbat and deliberate labors, and two sin offerings for the reaping and grinding of deliberate Shabbat violation and unintentional error about labors (Rivash/Rik"v, and see above 6:11).

but if he first became aware of the reaping of deliberate Shabbat violation and unintentional error about labors. And he is liable for this reaping to a sin offering separate from the sin offering he is liable for the grinding he did with it.
because both are like one labor. The reaping and grinding of unintentional error about Shabbat count as one labor, so that one sin offering atones for both.

and the reaping was drawn along with the reaping. The reaping of unintentional error about Shabbat is drawn after the reaping of unintentional error about labors and is atoned for with it (and the grinding is drawn along with it, since it and the reaping are like one labor).
these combine. Since there is one labor here, the half-measures combine to obligate a sin offering even though the errors are different.

one who intended to cut the detached and cut the attached. One who detaches is a derivative of reaping, and one is not liable unless he detached something attached to its place of growth (Hilchot Shabbat 8:3). This person wanted to cut something he thought was detached from the ground, and it turned out that he cut it while it was attached to the ground.
as we have explained several times. Above 2:7; Hilchot Shabbat 1:8-9.
if he intended to extinguish and to kindle he is liable to two. Two sin offerings, one for extinguishing and one for kindling.

he is liable because one is liable for a labor that is not needed for its own sake. Although he did the labor not for its main purpose but for a different purpose, he is liable. Therefore, although he did not intend to kindle but only to warm himself, he is liable to one sin offering for the kindling.
as we explained in Hilchot Shabbat. 1:7.
a fixed sin offering. But one who is uncertain whether he sinned in a sin for which one is liable to a variable burnt offering does not bring a provisional guilt offering (below 11:5).

because it atones for the doubt and holds it in suspense until it becomes known to him with certainty that he sinned unintentionally. Although it does not atone completely, since when he learns that he sinned he is liable to a sin offering, Scripture obligated this offering in order to calm the sinner's soul so that he not remain in fear because of the gravity of the sin about which he is in doubt (Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 6:3). Some explain that it holds in suspense to protect him from the suffering that comes to a sinner because of his sin (Rivash/Rik"v, Rabbeinu Gershom, Keritot 25a).
until there is a fixed prohibition. That there is no doubt about the existence of the prohibition; rather the doubt is whether the person actually committed a forbidden act for which he is liable.
Shabbat and a weekday: he did work on one of them and it is not known on which he did it. For example, he did a forbidden labor at twilight on Friday or at twilight at the end of Shabbat.

or he did an act on Shabbat and does not know which type of labor he did. He is uncertain whether the act he did is forbidden or permitted. But if he knows that he did a forbidden labor and is uncertain of which kind, he is exempt from a provisional guilt offering, since he knows he did a forbidden labor, and exempt from a sin offering because he does not know what his sin was (Lechem Mishneh, as above 2:3; see also below, halakhah 5, and so it implies in Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 4:3).
for there is no fixed prohibition here. For it is not certain that a forbidden piece was before him.

the fat of a koy. The koy is an animal defined as doubtfully a wild animal and doubtfully a domesticated animal; the fat of a wild animal is permitted to eat and the fat of a domesticated animal is forbidden to eat and carries karet. Thus the fat of a koy is forbidden out of doubt, and there is no fixed prohibition here (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 1:9, 1:13).
a doubtful niddah. Doubtfully impure, doubtfully pure.
a doubtful forbidden relation of blood kinship. Where it is uncertain whether she is forbidden to him by the prohibition of forbidden relations.

a woman on whose cloth blood was found after some time. She wiped herself after relations and found blood, but since she did not check immediately and waited a short time, it is uncertain whether she saw blood at the time of relations or afterwards (see above 5:6).

and one who marries his yevamah within three months and she gave birth, and it is not known whether it was a nine-month child of the first or a seven-month child of the last. The yavam must wait ninety days before performing levirate marriage with his brother's wife, out of concern that she is pregnant by his deceased brother (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:19). If he performed levirate marriage within three months and she gave birth, it is uncertain whether this child was born from the yavam (a seven-month child of the last) and the relations were permitted, or whether the child was born from the deceased brother (a nine-month child of the first), in which case the levirate relations were forbidden as relations with a brother's wife.
one who eats a piece. When there were two pieces before him, one of forbidden fat and one of permitted fat, and he ate one of them (Rik"v).
since the prohibition was fixed. For one of the pieces was forbidden fat.

and likewise anyone who has relations with a married woman about whom one witness says her husband died and another says he did not die. In this case this woman is forbidden to marry, and if she married she must be divorced because of the doubt (Hilchot Gerushin 12:19).
they are liable to a provisional guilt offering. For before their testimony this woman was presumed forbidden as a married woman, and there is a fixed prohibition here.

but with a doubtfully betrothed woman the prohibition was not fixed. For before her marriage she is presumed unmarried, and the doubt here is about the betrothal itself that establishes the prohibition.

or a gentile or a dog ate the first and an Israelite came and ate the second. Although in these cases there was one piece before the Israelite when he ate, it is considered a fixed prohibition because earlier there were two pieces and one of them was forbidden.

or he ate the first deliberately and the second unintentionally, or the first unintentionally and the second deliberately. For the deliberate eating he is liable to lashes or karet and not to a sin offering. And there is doubt whether the unintentional eating, which obligates a sin offering, was of the forbidden or the permitted piece.
ate both deliberately, he is exempt from an offering. Because it is certain that he ate the forbidden fat deliberately.
ate both unintentionally, he brings a sin offering. For it is certain that he ate forbidden fat unintentionally and there is no doubt here.
both are liable to a provisional guilt offering. For both are uncertain whether they ate forbidden fat unintentionally, and there was a fixed prohibition.
as we explained. Above 2:3.
just as if he ate forbidden fat, blood, notar and piggul in one lapse of awareness he is liable to four sin offerings. As above 6:4.
such-and-such forbidden relation that was with her, for which he is liable to eight sin offerings. For a case of one act of relations for which one is liable to eight sin offerings see above 4:2.

just as definite awareness in the interim divides for sin offerings. For example, he ate two olive-bulks of forbidden fat unintentionally in one lapse of awareness, then became aware of one olive-bulk, and again became aware of the second, he brings two sin offerings because the awarenesses divide (as above 6:9).

he is liable to a provisional guilt offering for each one. But if he became aware of the doubt about all of them together, he brings one provisional guilt offering for all (like the law of awareness regarding a sin offering).
he brings a sin offering. For he certainly ate forbidden fat.
as we said. Above, halakhah 4.
he brings a sin offering for the forbidden fat. For he certainly ate forbidden fat.
and a provisional guilt offering for notar. For he does not know whether he ate the piece of ordinary forbidden fat or the piece of forbidden fat that was notar.

ate the second in a second lapse of awareness, he brings three sin offerings. One sin offering for eating ordinary forbidden fat, and two sin offerings for eating the forbidden fat that was notar, for forbidden fat and for notar (and he is liable to two separate sin offerings for the forbidden fat because he ate the two pieces in separate lapses of awareness).

and if it was worth a perutah, he brings a definite guilt offering for misappropriation. For one who derives benefit from sacred meat worth a perutah or more pays what he benefited plus a fifth and is liable to a definite guilt offering (below 9:8, Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3).
for a designated maidservant. One who has relations with a designated maidservant, as explained below.
and for robbery. Below, halakhah 7.
and for misappropriation. Below, halakhot 8-9.

and for the impurity of a nazirite. When he became impure through one of the impurities he is warned against, he must bring on the eighth day a burnt offering, a sin offering and a lamb as a guilt offering (Hilchot Nezirut 6:11).

and for leprosy when he becomes pure of it. After the leper is healed and after his purification process, he must count seven days, and on the eighth day after his immersion he brings a burnt offering, a sin offering and a lamb as a guilt offering (below 10:3, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:1-2).

one who has relations with a designated maidservant. A designated maidservant is a Canaanite maidservant who is half slave and half free (for example, she belonged to two partners and one of them freed his share in her), who is betrothed to a Hebrew slave (Hilchot Ishut 4:17; Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 3:13; and see ibid. halakhot 14-17 for details of the laws of the designated maidservant corresponding to these).
whether deliberately or unintentionally. Unlike other forbidden relations, in which there is a difference between the deliberate and the unintentional.

provided that the maidservant is an adult, acting deliberately and willingly, and had been had relations with before. But if she was a minor, or acting unintentionally, or compelled, or asleep, or had not been had relations with before, he is exempt.

"there shall be an inquiry," etc. "and he shall bring his guilt offering": she is flogged and he brings an offering. The punishment of lashes is called here "inquiry" (for an explanation of the term see Commentary on the Mishnah, Keritot 2:5 and the commentators on the Torah), and because it says "there shall be," the Sages learned that it speaks of the woman alone, and the man brings a guilt offering (unlike the other forbidden relations, where the punishment of the man and the woman is equal).
and from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
and when she is exempt from lashes. For example, she was acting unintentionally or was a minor.
he is exempt from the offering. And in all the cases of exemption, the adult acting deliberately is given rabbinic lashes (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 3:16).

a boy of nine years and one day. Whose relations count as relations (see Hilchot Ishut 11:3). And because the maidservant is an adult and is flogged, he too is obligated in an offering. But if the maidservant was a minor (not yet twelve years and a day), she is exempt from lashes and therefore the man is exempt from the offering even if he is an adult.
we have already explained in Hilchot Bi'ot Assurot. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 3:13-15.
and they are not liable until he has relations in the normal way and completes. But if he had relations with her in an unnatural way, or only began and did not complete, he is exempt.

and what he said, "I did not have relations," meaning, "I did not complete". For we interpret his words in a way that does not deny the witnesses' words, and therefore he is exempt from the offering (see also above 3:1 and below 11:8).

even a hundred times in a hundred lapses of awareness, he offers one guilt offering and it atones for everything. Unlike other forbidden relations, where if he had relations with the forbidden woman several times in several lapses of awareness he is liable for each act of relations (above 5:1).
but one who has relations with many maidservants, even in one lapse of awareness, is liable to a guilt offering for each and every maidservant. Because there are separate bodies here.

for the law of the unintentional and the deliberate regarding a maidservant is the same. Since with a designated maidservant he is liable both deliberately and unintentionally, their law is the same regarding the division of guilt offerings. And just as in the deliberate case setting aside divides the offering (as explained in the previous passage), so in the unintentional case awareness alone does not divide, but only awareness accompanied by setting aside.

worth a perutah or more. But for less than the value of a perutah he is not liable to an offering for a false oath about a deposit, but he is liable to lashes for an oath of utterance (Hilchot Shevuot 7:16).
of an Israelite's money. But if he denied and swore falsely to a gentile about his money, he is exempt from an offering (compare Hilchot Gezelah 7:7).

and denied it and swore falsely, whether deliberately or unintentionally. The unintentional case here is where he was unaware that one is liable to an offering for this oath, although he knew it was forbidden and that he had his fellow's money; and the deliberate case is where he knew that one is liable to an offering for deliberately taking it. But if he forgot that he had his fellow's money or did not know that it is forbidden to swear falsely when denying money, he is compelled and exempt from an offering (Hilchot Shevuot 1:10-11).
and this is called the guilt offering for robberies. See also Hilchot Gezelah 7:1-2.

and it is explicit in the Torah that he is not atoned for by this guilt offering until he returns the money in his possession to its owners. For it says of the guilt offering: "the guilt offering to be returned to the Lord, to the priest, besides the ram of atonement by which atonement will be made for him" (Numbers 5:8), and the Sages learned that the guilt offering in the verse is the payment of the principal, and it says "by which atonement will be made" in the future tense to teach that atonement begins with returning the stolen item and is completed by bringing the offering (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 9:13).

but the fifth does not hold back the atonement. For the robber must return, besides the principal, an additional quarter of its value called the "fifth" (a fifth part added to the four parts of the principal), and this fifth does not hold back the atonement.
in Hilchot Shevuot. Chapters 7-8.
in Hilchot Me'ilah. 1:4.
dishes. Bowls.
even though they do not divide for the liability of karet. For example, he ate forbidden fat unintentionally from three dishes and is liable to only one sin offering (as above 6:1).

for he made the one who causes benefit like the one who benefits. For even one who feeds his fellow or causes him to benefit from sacred property is liable to a guilt offering for misappropriation (Hilchot Me'ilah 5:3).

and it combines over a long time. For if he ate or benefited from sacred property today to the value of half a perutah and after a long time to the value of half a perutah, in one lapse of awareness, they combine to a perutah and he is liable to a guilt offering for misappropriation (ibid. 5:4).

and an agent who carried out his agency, the sender is liable. For throughout the Torah there is no agent for a transgression and the agent is liable, but in misappropriation the sender is liable (ibid. 7:1-2).

but if he offered it before he became aware. For example, he was uncertain whether he misappropriated and brought a guilt offering on the condition that if he had misappropriated, this would be the guilt offering for his misappropriation.

and any sin for which one is liable to a definite guilt offering, the king, the anointed priest and the other people of the land are equal in it. Unlike the sin offering, where the offering of the king, the priest and the person of the land differ from one another (above 1:4), and unlike the provisional guilt offering, from which the anointed priest is exempt (as below 15:6).

exempt from everything. And he does not bring a provisional guilt offering, for the obligation to bring a provisional guilt offering applies only to doubt about a sin for which one is liable to a fixed sin offering for unintentional transgression (as above 8:1).
doubt about misappropriation. For example, two pieces were before him, one sacred and one ordinary, and he ate one of them and does not know which.
he is not liable for anything. Neither payment of the principal and the fifth, nor a guilt offering.
as we explained in Me'ilah. 1:5.
and a piece of sacred property. For eating it one is liable to a guilt offering for misappropriation.
he ate one of them and it is not known which, he is exempt. For one does not bring a provisional guilt offering for doubt about misappropriation.
he went and ate the second, he brings a guilt offering for his misappropriation. For he certainly ate the piece of sacred property.
both are exempt. For both are uncertain whether they ate the sacred piece.

ate the second, he brings a sin offering for the forbidden fat and a definite guilt offering for misappropriation for the sacred property. For he certainly ate forbidden fat and certainly ate sacred property.
another came and ate the second, the second also brings a provisional guilt offering. For regarding each of them there is doubt whether he ate the piece of forbidden fat.
ate one of them, he brings a sin offering. For he certainly ate forbidden fat.

he brings two sin offerings and a definite guilt offering for his misappropriation. For he ate two pieces of forbidden fat in two separate lapses of awareness, and ate sacred property. But if he ate in one lapse of awareness, he is liable to one sin offering for the two pieces of forbidden fat and a definite guilt offering for the sacred property.

this one brings a sin offering and this one brings only a sin offering. For eating the forbidden fat, and they are exempt from a guilt offering for misappropriation, since both are uncertain whether they ate the piece of sacred property.
in Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot. 14:19.

for what reason was the prohibition of sacred property added to the prohibition of forbidden fat. For forbidden fat is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit, and when he consecrated the animal, since a prohibition of benefit was added to this fat, the prohibition of eating sacred property was also added to it (an additional prohibition).
a variable offering. An offering whose type changes according to the means of the one offering it: a burnt offering with the rich and a lesser one with the poor.
and the woman after childbirth. Who brings an offering after the days of her purification are completed.

and one who swears an oath of testimony. Witnesses who know testimony in a monetary matter, and the one entitled to the testimony demanded that they testify for him, and they denied and swore that they know no testimony for him (Hilchot Shevuot 1:12).
whether deliberately or unintentionally. See above 9:7.

and one who swears an oath of utterance falsely unintentionally. One who swears falsely about something that was done or will be done, and knew that the oath is forbidden but did not know that one is liable to an offering for it, is considered to have acted unintentionally and is liable to a variable offering. But if he swore out of forgetfulness and the like, he is completely exempt (Hilchot Shevuot 3:6-8).

and it does not reach its libations. The libations are fine flour mixed with oil and wine that come together with the offering, and the offering of the woman after childbirth requires libations (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:2).
and a lamb for a guilt offering. For the guilt offering comes in every case only from male lambs and does not vary as a variable offering.
for an oath of testimony. Whether deliberately or unintentionally.
like the other fixed sin offerings. As above 1:4.
for their procedures have already been explained in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 12:4-9.

and it is explicit that he is obligated to bring them, except for an impure person who entered the Temple or ate sacred food, etc.. For Scripture explains only that a person who became impure has an obligation of an offering, but does not specify what he did after becoming impure; and from the fact that the Torah says one is liable to karet for entering the Temple in impurity or eating sacred food deliberately, the Sages learned that in these verses the Torah obligates an offering for the unintentional.
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

he brings on her behalf, and if he is poor he brings a poor person's offering, etc.. He is obligated to bring the offerings his wife is liable for, and because his wife is like his own body, the offering is judged according to the husband's financial situation (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 14:12).

and a person brings on behalf of his son, his daughter, his slave and his maidservant a poor person's offering. Even when he himself is rich, and in this case the judgment is according to the one for whom he brings.

and allows them to eat of the sacrifices. In cases where the person lacks atonement, bringing the offering by the father or master permits him to eat sacred food (see also Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:5).
ordinary people. The simple people.
as we explained. Above 1:4.
we have already explained in Hilchot Shevuot, etc.. Chapters 9-10 (oath of testimony), chapters 3-6 (oath of utterance).
and in Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah, etc.. 1:8 (woman after childbirth), 5:8 (leper).

anyone who brings an offering for a deliberate act as for an unintentional one. All the transgressions for which one transgressing either deliberately or unintentionally is liable to an offering: the guilt offering for robberies, the guilt offering for the designated maidservant and the variable offering for an oath of testimony (and although a nazirite who became impure is also liable for the deliberate as for the unintentional, he is an exception and is obligated even if compelled, since his offering does not come as atonement for a sin, see Hilchot Nezirut 6:3).
and he needed. A certain need arose for him to bring a she-goat in place of a lamb, for example he needed money and has a she-goat at home.
let him redeem those coins onto the she-goat and benefit from them. He transfers the sanctity of the coins to the she-goat, and the coins become unconsecrated and he may benefit from all of them.
he set aside coins for an animal and became poor. And wishes to bring a bird in its place.

let him take two turtledoves or two young pigeons and redeem those coins onto them and benefit from them. Instead of buying an animal with the coins he set aside, he redeems them onto a bird, and the remaining coins become unconsecrated and he may use them for his needs (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 5:9).
even if his bequeather was dying, etc.. And when he inherits he will be rich, this is not considered; rather we follow the person's financial situation at the time he brings the offering.

a rich person who set aside a lamb or a goat and a blemish fell in it. He set aside an animal while rich and a blemish fell in it and afterwards he became poor (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 5:10).
if he wishes, he may bring a bird with its value. And he may use the remaining coins for his needs.
and it was disqualified. For example, it became lacking a limb (for a blemish does not disqualify a bird).
for a bird has no redemption. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:4.

until he sanctified it in a vessel it is like all meal offerings. For before the meal offering is sanctified in a vessel it has the sanctity of value and may be redeemed. And all meal offerings not yet sanctified in a vessel are redeemed if they became impure or disqualified, and a sinner's meal offering can be redeemed even when it is pure (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:5).
and it is redeemed and eaten. He uses the redemption money to buy the offering of a rich person, and the flour is eaten.

its form shall pass and it shall go to the place of burning. One must wait until the meal offering spoils and is no longer fit for eating and then burn it in the place where disqualified sacred items are burned.

because what is rejected from the start is not rejected, and this nest is now fit for him. There is a rule concerning sacred things (whether sanctity of the body or sanctity of value) that something that was fit for offering and was rejected because of a certain disqualification is disqualified entirely even if the cause of disqualification no longer exists ("seen and rejected does not return and become seen"). However, when from the beginning the thing was not fit for offering, then when it becomes fit it is offered ("what is rejected from the beginning is not rejected"; see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:22-24 and the commentary there). Therefore, since this nest was not fit for offering by him when he was rich, it is not rejected, and now it is fit for offering.
for all the karet penalties, etc.. As above 2:6.
awareness of the impurity and awareness of the sacred food or the Temple at the beginning. That he was aware that he became impure and also that he is eating sacred food or entering the Temple.

of these six divisions. Unawareness of the impurity and awareness of the sacred food or Temple; awareness of the impurity and unawareness of the sacred food or Temple; unawareness of the impurity and unawareness of the sacred food or Temple (and "unawareness" includes forgetting the law, such as forgetting that it is forbidden to enter the Temple or eat sacred meat in impurity).
and it is said, "and he knows". From this we learn that awareness is needed at the end, after it was hidden from him.
by which primary source of impurity. Of the primary sources of impurity that convey impurity.

since he knew that he was impure, there was awareness of impurity at the beginning. For there is no need for exact awareness of which kind of impurity he contracted, but general awareness that he became impure suffices.

that he became impure through a lentil-size amount of a creeping thing. The eight creeping things mentioned in the Torah are among the primary sources of impurity and convey impurity by contact if one touched an amount the size of a lentil of them (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 4:1-2).

it is doubtful whether he is liable to an offering or exempt. For on one hand he knows that a creeping thing conveys impurity, but on the other hand he does not know the amount that conveys impurity, and we are uncertain whether awareness of the fact without awareness of the law counts as awareness.
and likewise one who never saw the Temple in his life and did not understand its location. But knows that there is a Temple in the world.

lest they bring ordinary food into the Temple court.
