For a sin offering does not come as a vow or a freewill offering but only for a sin (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:8), and if a person brings a sin offering he is not obligated to bring, he brings ordinary food into the court (for this prohibition see Hilchot Shechitah 2:1-3).

but does not the bird sin offering come out of doubt and is not eaten. For example, a doubtful zavah or doubtful woman after childbirth brings a bird sin offering out of doubt (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 7:10).

because the one who brings it lacks atonement and is forbidden to eat sacred food until he brings his atonement. Only those lacking atonement (the zav, zavah, woman after childbirth and leper) bring a bird sin offering out of doubt, since they are forbidden to eat sacred food until they bring their offering, and if they were not permitted to offer a sin offering out of doubt they would not be permitted to eat sacred food (and a nazirite also brings a sin offering out of doubt because his offering permits him to drink wine and to cut his hair - see Hilchot Nezirut 9:15).
one who became impure in the Temple court. His law is that he must hurry and leave by the short way, and he may not remain there or bow or leave by the long way (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:21-22).
when he becomes aware, let him bring a variable offering. For he had awareness of the impurity and awareness of the Temple at the beginning.

provided that he remained for the measure, as we explained in Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash. 3:23. There it was explained that the measure that obligates is the time of bowing, and its measure is the time to recite the verse "and they bowed with their faces to the ground on the pavement, and prostrated themselves and gave thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His kindness endures forever" (II Chronicles 7:3).

it is doubtful whether the measure of bowing applies only to one who is compelled or also to one who acts deliberately. And if the measure is only for one who is compelled, then the deliberate transgressor would be liable even if he did not remain the measure of bowing.

and therefore if it became hidden from him and he left and did not remain. For example, immediately after deliberately making himself impure the impurity became hidden from him and he then left the court without remaining.

it is doubtful whether the airspace of the court is like the court or is not like the court. Perhaps the remaining for which one is liable is remaining in which there is a practical possibility of bowing (Lechem Mishneh, based on Tosafot Shevuot 17a).

one impure. For example, the width of the path has a grave that one walking on it must necessarily overshadow and thereby become impure, and it is not clear which path is pure and which path is impure.
and entered the Temple or ate sacred food. And afterwards he learned that he walked on both paths and that he is impure.
for a part of awareness is like all awareness. The awareness of walking on the second path, which is partial awareness of his impurity, suffices to be called awareness at the beginning.
walked on the first. On the first path only, and there is no certainty at all that he became impure.

sprinkled on the third and seventh and immersed after entering the Temple. After walking on the first path and entering the Temple in doubtful impurity, he sprinkled on himself on the third and seventh days the waters of the sin offering to purify himself from doubtful corpse impurity, and immersed.
and walked on the second and again entered the Temple. After his immersion he walked on the second path, it was hidden from him that he walked, and he entered the Temple.
for if he wishes he can say: I was deliberate. And therefore we interpret his words as if he said "I was deliberate" and there is no denial in his words, and he is exempt from the offering.

since he denied the witnesses and said, "I never became impure," these are believed and he brings an offering on their word. Although in the previous case we interpret his words in a way that does not deny the witnesses and he is exempt, in this case his statement "I never became impure" does not allow interpreting his words otherwise, and therefore he is denying the witnesses and is liable. But if he had said "I did not enter," it could be interpreted that he meant he did not enter in impurity but in purity, and he would be exempt (Kesef Mishneh, and see also above 3:1, above 9:4).
the goat of Yom Kippur that is done inside. The goat on which the lot fell for the Lord, whose blood is sprinkled in the Sanctuary and the Holy of Holies.
and that has no awareness at the beginning but has awareness at the end. And in this case he is exempt from a variable burnt offering, as above, halakhah 1.
the goat done outside on Yom Kippur. A sin offering goat offered on Yom Kippur on the outer altar as part of the additional offerings.
the goats of the festivals and the goats of the new moons. The sin offering goat that is offered on these occasions as part of the additional offerings.
and for deliberate impurity of the Temple and its sacred things. That he was impure and ate sacred food or entered the Temple deliberately.

the bull of the High Priest on Yom Kippur. The sin offering bull that the High Priest brings on Yom Kippur from his own property, and sprinkles from its blood in the Sanctuary as part of the day's service.
anything for whose unintentional transgression one is liable to a fixed sin offering. These are the forty-three karet transgressions enumerated above (1:4).
and they ruled to permit it. They ruled the wrong law to the people, unintentionally.
and the people erred in their ruling. According to their ruling.
and they rely on their ruling. But one who did not rely in his act on the court's ruling, but erred for another reason (as below 13:5), must bring a sin offering himself for his sin.
for no heed is paid at all to the court's act. The bringing of the offering does not depend on their act but on their ruling.

they bring a bull for a burnt offering and a goat for a sin offering from each and every tribe. For the obligation of the offering is on the court, but the offering is brought from the community's funds (and for this a special collection is made - Hilchot Shekalim 4:2).

and if it was hidden from the eyes of the congregation, done unintentionally. And Scripture concludes: "then all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering... and one male goat for a sin offering."
and if the whole congregation of Israel errs. And Scripture concludes: "then the assembly shall offer a young bull for a sin offering."
and they are burned. Outside the Temple (for the burning procedure see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:2).

for their blood is brought inside. For their blood is brought into the Sanctuary and sprinkled from it on the curtain and on the golden altar, and a sin offering whose blood is brought inside is burned (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:13-16).
as it is said, "and the assembly shall offer". In the passage on the hidden matter of the community.
as it is said, "and Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah". From this verse they learned that the tribe of Judah, although it is one tribe, is called an "assembly" (Talmud Horayot 5b).

for even those who did not sin bring on behalf of those who sinned. For the liability for the offering depends on the act of the majority, and the minority who did not sin take part in the collection for the offerings.
on behalf of. For the sake of.
as will be explained. Below 14:4.
in what case is this said, etc.. These conditions will be explained at length in the coming chapters.
the head of the academy. The one greater in wisdom than the other members of the Sanhedrin, whom they seat as head over them (Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:3).
and all of them err. All the members of the court.

or most of them. And the minority are silent and do not say that in their opinion the majority are erring in the law; but if the minority stated their opinion, the court members are exempt and those who acted are liable (below 13:1).

you are permitted to do. But if they said only "this thing is permitted," this is not an explicit ruling to act and therefore does not obligate the court, but those who acted are liable to a sin offering (ibid.).
if they told others, let them say to them: you are permitted to do. Explicitly, as they heard from the court.

and they ruled to nullify part and uphold part, not that they uproot the whole body. That they ruled erroneously regarding one of the laws that are not explained and explicit in the Torah, but not in a fundamental law that uproots one of the bodies of the Torah (below 14:1).

they knew the matter itself in which they ruled unintentionally. But if it was hidden from them which law they ruled erroneously, the court members are exempt and those who acted are liable (below 14:4).
if the High Court ruled... that the forbidden fat of the stomach is permitted. And in truth it is one of the forbidden fats that carry karet (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 7:6).

that court is exempt and everyone who ate brings a fixed sin offering for his unintentional transgression. Because this was the court of a particular tribe that ruled for a particular tribe, and not the High Court that ruled for all Israel.

if the High Court ruled that the blood of the heart is permitted. And in truth it is forbidden with karet (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 6:3; see also below 14:2, that if they ruled that the blood of slaughter is permitted, in every case they are exempt).
and the head of the academy was not with them. Even if their number was complete, seventy-one (Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 1:4).
for example, he was a convert or a mamzer, etc.. For the list of people not fit to be appointed to the Sanhedrin see Hilchot Sanhedrin chapter 2.

an old man who has not seen children. An elderly man who never had children. Because he does not know the love of children, his heart is hard and he has no mercy on people (Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 1:4; and a very aged man, even if he had children and they died, is disqualified, since he tends to cruelty because of his age - see Hilchot Sanhedrin 2:3).
and from where do we learn that Scripture speaks only of the High Court. And not of the court of a single tribe.
as it is said, "and if the whole congregation of Israel errs". From this we learn that it speaks of a court that is able to rule for all Israel and not for one tribe only.
and from where do we learn that until all of them are fit to rule. And not that the head of the academy is missing or one of them was unfit to be appointed to the Sanhedrin.
until they have, as it were, eyes. From this we learn that if the head of the academy, who is like eyes for them, was not with them, the court members are exempt (see Jerusalem Talmud Horayot 1:4).
and below it says, "and the congregation shall judge". This verse was said in the passage on the unintentional killer judged in court, and from it we learn that all of them must be fit to rule.
and they were silent. They did not say before the court that in their opinion the court was erring.

if they acted according to those who ruled, they are liable, because they did not rely on the court. For only one who relies on the court absolutely is exempt, but if he knew that they erred and acted on their word because he thought it a commandment to listen to the court, he is liable (as below, halakhah 5).

for only the people of the Land of Israel are called an assembly. For the bull for a hidden matter of the community is called the "sin offering of the assembly," and from this it comes only when the whole assembly or its majority erred. And this majority is determined by the majority of the tribes or the majority of the people in the Land of Israel, for only they are called an assembly, as learned from the verse: "And Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt" (I Kings 8:65; Talmud Horayot 3a).
they are not counted as two tribes for this purpose. But only for the inheritance of the land (Commentary on the Mishnah, Introduction to Horayot).

the actors were a majority at the time of the sin and a minority at the time of awareness. For example, some of the majority who sinned died, and when the error became known it turned out that those who did not sin are the majority.

or a minority at the time of the sin and a majority at the time of awareness. For example, some of the majority who did not sin died, and when the error became known it turned out that those who sinned are the majority.
everything follows the time of the act. We judge according to the status of majority and minority at the time the sin was committed.

these combine. Although these are different transgressions whose offerings differ, the two minorities combine together, so that a majority of the congregation acted according to the court's rulings, and the court is obligated to bring an offering on behalf of the community (Kesef Mishneh; and see the rulings and opinions about which offering the court brings).
even though they had awareness in the interim. That they learned that they erred in the first ruling before they gave the second ruling.
these do not combine with those. And the court is exempt from an offering, and the individuals are liable to bring a sin offering.

because it occurred to him that it is a commandment to listen to the court even though they err. He thought he was obligated to listen to their ruling even when they err and he recognizes their error, because it says: "According to the law that they teach you and according to the judgment they tell you, you shall do; you shall not turn aside from the word that they declare to you, to the right or to the left" (Deuteronomy 17:11; Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 1:1).
and he is not counted in the number of those who erred by their word. He is not included in the count of those who erred when counting whether there was a majority or a minority.
for his awareness of the prohibition is not definite awareness. And therefore this awareness does not make him count as acting on his own, but as acting on the court.

and it is not fit to accept from them. But if the community erred because they thought it a commandment to listen to the court's words even in this case, the community is liable and the court is exempt (as above regarding an individual; Rik"v, and so it is proven in Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 1:5).
and they ruled to uproot a body of the Torah. That they ruled to permit one of the prohibitions of the Torah.

until they rule to nullify part and uphold part. The court's liability applies when their ruling is not a complete uprooting of one of the Torah's prohibitions, but an uprooting of one of the details of the prohibition.

in matters that are not explicit and explained in the Torah. But if they forgot a verse of the Torah, or something with such strong support in Scripture that even the Sadducees agree to it, even if it is only a detail, the court is exempt and those who acted are liable (Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 1:3).

a woman guarding day for day. A woman who sees blood during the days of her zivah for one day or two must immerse and guard a day of clean blood, and on that day she is forbidden to have relations (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:7).

these are as if they said there is no Shabbat in the Torah... that they uprooted the whole body. Even if they ruled a permission in one of the laws of Shabbat or idolatry or niddah, since it is explicit in the Torah and they canceled it entirely, it is considered an uprooting of the whole body.
but one who throws or passes is permitted. And in truth one who passes or throws is liable (Hilchot Shabbat 12:10).
these are liable. For this is not an uprooting of a law explicit in the Torah, but of a particular detail within the definitions of this law.

or they uprooted a primary labor of the labors and ruled that it is not a labor, these are liable. For the primary labors of Shabbat are not explicitly defined in the Torah as "labor" forbidden on Shabbat (except the labor of carrying out - see Hilchot Shabbat 12:8), and therefore this is not considered an uprooting of a body of the Torah.
by spreading hands and feet. That he prostrates himself completely on the ground, which is the bowing mentioned in the Torah (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 6:6; see also Hilchot Tefillah 5:13).

but one who kneels on the ground and did not spread his hands and feet is permitted. And in truth even without spreading hands and feet, from the moment he kneeled and pressed his face to the ground he is liable (Hilchot Avodah Zarah, ibid. halakhah 8).

for one whose wife became a niddah during relations is permitted to withdraw from her at that moment while he is erect. And in truth the law is that he must remain until the organ is soft (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:11; see also above 5:7).

that one who eats blood that came out at slaughter is the one liable, but one who eats the blood of the heart is permitted: these are liable. For blood that comes out at slaughter is blood in which the life departs, and its prohibition derives from the plain wording of Scripture: "for the life of all flesh is its blood; whoever eats it shall be cut off" (Leviticus 17:14). But the prohibition of the blood of the heart is not explicit in Scripture.

this is not a ruling but an error, and the woman and her last husband are liable to a sin offering for their unintentional transgression. When these are individual cases, there is no need to say that the court is exempt and those who act according to them are liable, for if an individual or a minority acted on the court's ruling, the individuals are liable (as above 13:1); rather, even if those acting were the majority of Israel, the court is exempt and those who acted are liable, because this is not a ruling but an error (Lechem Mishneh, above 5:5).
since they learned. After the court learned that they erred in their ruling.

this is as one who was uncertain whether he sinned or did not sin. For on one hand he relied in his act on the court's ruling, and one who relies on the court is exempt; on the other hand, since he is in the country and has a duty to find out whether the ruling is still valid, he can be considered one who relied on himself, who is liable to a sin offering. So there is doubt here and he is obligated to a provisional guilt offering.

except one who hurries to leave, even though he has not yet set out on the road... he is exempt. Since he is busy with his journey and cannot ask, it is as if he is in another country (Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 1:2).
we have already explained. Above 1:4.
an anointed priest. A High Priest anointed with the anointing oil (see below, halakhah 7).
provided that he is an outstanding sage. One fit to rule on the whole Torah (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 4:8).
erred and threw unintentionally. Not because he thought it was permitted but because he forgot that throwing is forbidden on Shabbat, or it was hidden from him that it was Shabbat.

or he uprooted a whole body by his ruling for himself. For example, he ruled for himself that it is permitted to carry from domain to domain on Shabbat, which is considered an uprooting of the whole body for which the court is exempt (above 14:2).

or he erred in a ruling to nullify part and did not act relying on his ruling but acted through another error. For example, he ruled for himself that it is permitted to eat the forbidden fat of the stomach, which is not an uprooting of the whole body, and when he ate he did not rely on his ruling but ate because of a mistake, for example he intended to eat permitted fat and ate the fat of the stomach (above 13:5).

he is completely exempt from an offering. Although in these cases, if an individual had acted on the court's ruling he would be liable to a sin offering, the law of the anointed priest is different and he is completely exempt.

for his law regarding his own ruling is the same as the law of the community regarding the court's ruling in every respect. And just as the court is exempt in these cases from bringing an offering on behalf of the community, so the anointed priest is exempt.

he ruled for himself and forgot for what reason he ruled. Although one could say that had he remembered the reason for his ruling he would have retracted and he could therefore be considered deliberate, since he acted according to his ruling he is considered unintentional and is liable to a sin offering (Talmud Horayot 6b).

he brings a she-goat like an ordinary person. For in unintentional idolatry the offering of all is the same and there is no distinction between an ordinary person, a king or an anointed priest (as above 1:4).
provided that he erred in a ruling as we explained. Above, halakhot 1-2.
like the community. Like the offering that the court brings on behalf of the community when the court erred in a ruling and the majority acted according to it.
but if he erred in an act alone without a ruling. He erred without a mistaken ruling for himself having preceded it.

the anointed priest ruled together with the court and he and they erred in a ruling. The anointed priest was in the same place as the court, the court ruled for the community and he ruled for himself regarding the same prohibition.
except if the court was bringing an offering. For example, those who sinned by the court's ruling were the majority of Israel.
and if the actors were the ones bringing the offering. For example, those who sinned by the court's ruling were a minority of Israel.

and they erred about blood and he about forbidden fat. The anointed priest was in the same place as the court, and they ruled a permission for blood for the community and he ruled a permission for forbidden fat for himself.

he is not atoned for with the community but brings a bull for himself. Although his ruling for himself was in the presence of the court, we do not say that he relied on the fact that the court heard his ruling and did not protest, and consider him as one who relied on the court, but he is defined as one who ruled for himself (Rabbeinu Chananel, Horayot 9a).
because in it he is like the community. Like a court, which is exempt from a provisional guilt offering in this case (as above 12:2).

because his unintentional error does not depend on a ruling. Although there is a difference between the prince and an individual in the type of offering brought for unintentional karet transgressions, in the provisional guilt offering there is no difference between them, since the prince is not like the court, whose offering does not depend on ruling.
and none of them serves his fellow; each and every one of them brings a goat for his unintentional error. Because he is not subordinate to the other kings, he is defined as a prince.

not one invested with the garments. At a time when there is no anointing oil, the High Priest is appointed to his office ("invested") by wearing the eight garments of the High Priest (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:12-13). And a priest appointed in this way has the same law as a High Priest anointed with the anointing oil, except for the law of the bull for the unintentional error of an anointed priest, which does not apply to one invested with the garments (ibid. halakhah 14).

and the like. For example, they appointed him as a replacement for the High Priest who suffered a disqualification on Yom Kippur, and afterwards the first priest returned to his service (Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 3:4).

brings a bull for his unintentional error. Because the effect of the anointing oil with which he was anointed is not annulled, unlike a prince who left his princely office and whose law is that of an ordinary person, since his greatness depends on his being a prince in practice (as below, halakhah 9; Commentary on the Mishnah, Horayot 3:2).
the bull of Yom Kippur. The bull the High Priest brings on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1).
and the tenth of the ephah of each day. The griddle-cake meal offering that the High Priest is commanded to offer every day with the daily offering (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:18).
the bull that comes for all the commandments. The bull that an anointed priest offers for his unintentional error in his own ruling.
as we explained. Above 12:1.
he brings a goat. For unintentional error in the other karet transgressions, and in idolatry he brings a she-goat like an ordinary person (as above 1:4).

for his sin which he has sinned. The commentators found it difficult to derive this from this verse, since it speaks of the anointed priest and not the prince. Some wrote that there may be a slip of language here and the intent is the verse said of the prince: "or his sin which he has sinned is made known to him" (Leviticus 4:23; see Rik"v and Tosafot Yom Tov, Horayot 3:1), and others wrote that the law of the prince is learned from the anointed priest (Horeh Gever, Horayot 10a).

he does not combine and is exempt. For his offering when he was an ordinary person is not the same as his offering when he was a prince, and therefore the eatings do not combine to one measure, and he is completely exempt and brings neither a goat nor a she-goat.
and he was appointed and passed from office. He was appointed prince and afterwards left his princely office.

it is doubtful whether he combines or whether the princely office already interrupted. It is doubtful whether, since both eatings were while he was an ordinary person and his offering at those times is the same, they combine, or perhaps the princely office constitutes an interruption between the eatings, and he brings no offering at all.
